title: Where, and what
prompt:
Most error messages have two halves. Click the part of this one that tells
you *what* went wrong.
hint: One part names the code R was running. The other describes the problem.

options.feedback:
Right. After the colon is the *what*: R couldn't find a package by that
name — here because it's misspelled. Before the colon is the *where*:
the call R was running when it stopped.

Reading them in that order — what, then where — is the quickest way
into any error. The *what* tells you the kind of problem; the *where*
tells you which line to look at.

This is the *where*: the call R was running when it stopped. Useful for
finding the line, but the description of the problem comes after the
colon.

Every error starts this way — it's just R announcing an error. The
useful parts come after it: which call, and then what went wrong.

title: A line R couldn't read
prompt:
```r
sbp <- c(118, 142 131, 156)
```

```
Error: unexpected numeric constant in "sbp <- c(118, 142 131"
```

Did any of this line run?
hint:
"Unexpected" means R was reading the line and hit something it didn't
expect.

options.text: No — R couldn't read the line, so none of it ran
options.feedback:
Right. This is a *syntax* error: the line isn't written in a way R can
read, so R never starts running it. `sbp` wasn't created or changed.

"Unexpected" is the giveaway. And R quotes your line up to the exact
point where it got confused — it stopped at `131`, so the mistake is
just before it: a missing comma after `142`.

options.text: Yes — `sbp` was created with the first two values
options.feedback:
R reads a whole line before running any of it. It couldn't make sense
of this one, so nothing ran — `sbp` doesn't exist.

options.text: Yes — `sbp` was created, but 131 was skipped
options.feedback:
R never skips part of a line it can't read. A syntax error means the
whole line is rejected, and nothing runs.

title: Code copied from a document
prompt:
You copied this line from a slide deck:

```
site <- “north”
```

```
Error: unexpected input in "site <- “"
```

What's wrong?
hint:
R quotes the line up to the point where it got confused. Look very closely
at the last character it quotes.

options.text: The quotation marks are curly, not straight
options.feedback:
Right. Word processors, slides, emails and PDFs turn straight quotes
`"` into curly ones “ ”, and R only understands the straight kind. The
two look almost identical, which is why this catches people so often.

It's worth knowing because copying code out of a document is exactly
how a lot of code reaches you. Retype the quotes and it runs.

options.text: `site` is a word R reserves for itself
options.feedback:
`site` is an ordinary name. R got as far as `site <- ` without trouble;
it stopped at the quotation mark.

options.text: `north` needs to be a number
options.feedback:
Text is fine in a variable — it just needs the right quotes around it.
R stopped at the quotation mark itself.

title: An else on its own
hint:
You met this in module 11. Where does the `else` sit, compared with the
`}` before it?

options.text: `else` has to come straight after the `}`, on the same line
options.feedback:
Right. When R reaches the `}` on its own line, it decides the `if` is
finished. So the next line seems to start with `else` out of nowhere,
which is a syntax error. Write `} else {` on one line and it works.

It's an R quirk, and generated code gets it wrong more often than
you'd think.

options.text: The `else` block needs more than one line in it
options.feedback:
One line is fine. The trouble is where `else` sits: R had already
decided the `if` was finished at the `}`.

options.text: R doesn't allow `else` after an `if`
options.feedback:
It does — you read one in module 11. It just has to follow the `}` on
the same line.

title: A bracket that never closes
prompt:
This gives `Error: unexpected end of input` — R reached the end of the
line still waiting for a bracket to close. Fix it so it works out each
patient's MAP.

MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3
hint:
Count the brackets that open and the brackets that close. Then think about
*where* the missing one goes — the division should apply to the whole top
part of the formula.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

solution.why:
The missing bracket goes after `patients$dbp`, so the division by 3
applies to the whole of `sbp + 2 × dbp`. R can read the line now, and
the formula is the one you wanted.

checks.on_fail:
The MAPs aren't right yet. Check that the division applies to the
whole of the top part of the formula.

misconceptions.feedback:
There's still a bracket that never closes. Count them: every `(` needs
a `)`.

No error now — R can read the line — but look at the answer: 200.67 for
a patient at 142/88. The bracket closes in the wrong place, so only the
diastolic part is divided by 3. That's the same mistake from module 9.

This is worth sitting with. Fixing an error means R can run your code.
It doesn't mean the code does what you meant. That's module 14.

title: What ran before it stopped
prompt:
This stops with an error on the third line:

```r
weight <- 70
height <- "1.75"
bmi <- weight / (height * height)
```

```
Error in height * height : non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

Afterwards, which of these exist?
hint:
R runs a script one line at a time, top to bottom. What had already
happened when it reached the third line?

options.text: `weight` and `height` — but not `bmi`
options.feedback:
Right. R runs line by line, and stops at the first error. Everything
before it has already happened — `weight` and `height` were stored.
The line that failed stored nothing, so `bmi` doesn't exist.

That matters when you re-run part of a script: some things will already
be there from last time, and some won't.

options.text: None of them — the script failed
options.feedback:
A script isn't all-or-nothing. The first two lines ran and stored their
values before R reached the error.

options.text: All three, with `bmi` set to `NA`
options.feedback:
An error doesn't give you an `NA` — it stops. The line that failed
stored nothing at all, so `bmi` doesn't exist.

title: Where it broke, and why
prompt:
The error names `height * height`, on the third line. Click the line that
actually *caused* it.

```
Error in height * height : non-numeric argument to binary operator
```
hint:
"Non-numeric argument" means one side of the `*` isn't a number. Why isn't
it?

options.feedback:
Right. The quotes made `height` text, back on the second line. R only
noticed on the third, when it tried to multiply.

That's the general rule: an error tells you where R *noticed* the
problem, which isn't always where the problem *is*. When the line it
names looks fine, look at where its ingredients came from.

This is where R *noticed* the problem, and it's the line the error
names. But the formula is fine. It was handed text instead of a number
— so where did that text come from?
`weight` is a proper number. The other ingredient is the problem.

title: A warning isn't an error
prompt:
```r
labs <- c("12.4", "<5", "31.0")
crp  <- as.numeric(labs)
mean(crp, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```
Warning message:
NAs introduced by coercion
[1] 21.7
```

Did the code finish?

options.text: Yes — a warning lets R carry on, and the mean is 21.7
options.feedback:
Right. A warning isn't an error: R finishes, but flags that something
happened you might want to know about. Here, `"<5"` couldn't become a
number, so it turned into `NA` — and then `na.rm = TRUE` quietly left
it out. The mean is of 12.4 and 31.0 only.

Warnings sit between the two kinds of failure: the code ran, but R is
telling you something. They're easy to scroll past. Module 14 is about
problems that don't even warn you.

options.text: No — it stopped at the warning
options.feedback:
A warning never stops R. Only an error does. The `[1] 21.7` underneath
is the finished result.

options.text: Yes, and the mean includes all three values
options.feedback:
It finished, but not with all three. The warning says an `NA` was
introduced: `"<5"` couldn't become a number, and `na.rm = TRUE` then
left it out. 21.7 is the mean of 12.4 and 31.0.

title: could not find function
prompt:
```
Error in select(patients, age) : could not find function "select"
```

What's the most likely fix?

options.text: `library(dplyr)`
options.feedback:
Right. dplyr is installed but not loaded in this session. The error is
honest here, because base R has no `select()` of its own.

Compare module 12, where forgetting `library(dplyr)` before `filter()`
gave a misleading `object 'sbp' not found`. Base R *does* have a
`filter()`, so a different one ran. Same mistake, two very different
messages.

options.text: `install.packages("dplyr")`
options.feedback:
If dplyr weren't installed, you'd get "there is no package called…"
when you tried to load it. "Could not find function" usually means it
just isn't loaded.

options.text: Check the spelling of `patients`
options.feedback:
The error names the function, `select`, not the data. R never got as
far as looking at `patients`.

title: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
prompt:
```
Error in if (reading > 140) print("high") :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```

What's the most likely cause?
hint:
The message says something that should be TRUE or FALSE was missing.
Which kind of value is neither?

options.text: A missing value reached the `if`, so `reading > 140` was `NA`
options.feedback:
Right — module 11's loop. `NA > 140` is `NA`, and `if` needs a definite
TRUE or FALSE. So when you see this message, look for missing values in
whatever feeds the `if`.

Its close relative is *the condition has length > 1*: that one means
the `if` was given a whole column instead of a single value. The fix
there is usually `ifelse()`.

options.text: `TRUE` or `FALSE` is misspelled somewhere
options.feedback:
Nothing is misspelled. The message means the comparison came out as
`NA`, which is neither TRUE nor FALSE.

options.text: The data frame is empty
options.feedback:
The message is about a single missing value — `reading` was `NA` on
one pass of the loop. The data can be full apart from that one.

title: replacement has 3 rows
prompt:
```
Error in `$<-.data.frame`(`*tmp*`, dbp, value = c(88, 76, 82)) :
  replacement has 3 rows, data has 5
```

The first line looks alarming. What does the error actually mean?
hint: Skip the first line and read the second.

options.text: The new column was given three values, but there are five patients
options.feedback:
Right — module 9's rule. A single value would fill every row, but
several values have to match the number of patients exactly.

And the first line is worth decoding once. `$<-.data.frame` is R's
internal name for storing into a column with `$`, and `*tmp*` is a
placeholder it uses along the way. When the *where* looks like that,
it's R's own machinery — go straight to the *what*.

options.text: Two patients' rows have gone missing from the data
options.feedback:
All five patients are still there — "data has 5". The problem is the
new column: three values for five rows.

options.text: Something called `*tmp*` is broken
options.feedback:
`*tmp*` is a placeholder R uses internally when storing into a column.
It's not your problem. The message after the colon is.

title: undefined columns selected
prompt:
This gives `undefined columns selected`. Fix it so it returns the blood
pressure column.
hint:
Compare the column name with the names in the **Data** panel, character by
character.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

solution.why:
There's no column called `SBP` — capitals count — so R stopped rather
than guess. "Undefined columns selected" nearly always means a column
name that doesn't match exactly.

checks.on_fail: That isn't the blood pressure column yet.

misconceptions.feedback:
Still no column by that name. Compare it with the **Data** panel —
capitals count.

Inside square brackets, a column name needs quotes. Without them, R
looks for a variable called `sbp`.

No error this time — but you got `NULL`, nothing at all. `$` with a
wrong name fails *silently*, where the square brackets at least stopped
you. That's exactly the kind of problem module 14 is about. The column
is `sbp`, in lower case.

title: Asking for help with an error
prompt:
You're stuck on an error you don't understand. Which of these gives a
search engine or an AI the best chance of helping?
hint: The message says what went wrong. What else would someone need to know?

options.text: The exact error message, plus the lines of code that produced it
options.feedback:
Right. The message says *what* went wrong; the code shows *where* and
*why*. With both, an AI can usually point at the line. For a search
engine, the message itself — in quotes, with "R" — finds other people
who hit the same thing.

One firm rule: share the code and the error, never real patient data.
If the problem depends on what the data looks like, describe its
shape — the column names and types — without the values. Module 16 is
about exactly that.

options.text: "My R code doesn't work"
options.feedback:
There's nothing here to go on. The error message is the most useful
thing you have — it says exactly what kind of problem it is.

options.text: The whole script, without the error message
options.feedback:
Better than nothing, but whoever's helping has to guess what went
wrong. The message tells them straight away.

options.text: The error message with the names changed to something general
options.feedback:
Keeping the message exact is what makes it searchable. The names in it
are rarely private — `sbp` and `patients` identify no one. What *is*
private is the data itself, and that's what to keep out.
